utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you, too. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together within a team with Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us here our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Are there any preliminaries this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher can escort the witness into the courtroom, please. How long do you expect your cross-examination to last, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A couple of hours, Your Honour, certainly before the end of the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just to put you on the alert, we need the first break to be of something like 40 minutes' duration. And then we will talk about the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. We are proceeding with your testimony today, and it's the turn of the Prosecution with their cross-examination. Now, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I have questions for you this morning, and I will start right away. Yesterday you gave testimony regarding your mission going to the north of Bosnia from Sarajevo, and the aim, the initial aim, was Tuzla. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you undergo any briefing about the situation there in Sarajevo by, let's say, UNMO?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefing on Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I just followed on TV. We had TV in Sarajevo, but I had no briefing on the exact situation in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There's no guideline for giving briefings to UNMOs heading for some missions and updating them of the situation from headquarters point of view or sitreps?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been briefed in Tuzla, by the people in Tuzla. The people in Sarajevo don't necessarily know what's going on in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I see. Now, you arrived in -- not in Tuzla but entered near Zvornik. And had you been briefed there by the team leader, that's Alex Vassiliev?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefed -- well, I met him that evening when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. I mean briefed about the situation.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In Zvornik or Tuzla. And then I mean the military situation.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That evening when I did meet him he briefed me on the situation, particularly in Konjevic Polje that day. And once I -- once it was determined that I would be staying at that team the next day, then I immediately started reading into the situation, especially as the two IC of the team, I had to start finding out what was going on as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The situation in Konjevic Polje, meaning also the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much of the situation as we could find out in the Zvornik bridge area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. What was the update regarding these forces at various sites, Serb forces, in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he particularly told me about the incident in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But because we could not get into a lot of the areas because they refused our entry to where we wanted to go and we were supposed to have freedom of movement, then in many cases we could only speculate. Or if we actually saw things, like I mentioned yesterday, then that would be part of building the information situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, there came a time that you went to Srebrenica. You were aiming -- you were trying to get there, and finally the 27th of March you were able to get to Srebrenica. Were you also updated by this team leader regarding the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because he was not in Srebrenica. So he -- we were unable to get any information other than from the people that were inside, General Morillon, a few military observers. But due to what I said yesterday, the fact that we had poor radio communications, then we didn't know a lot from anybody else. It all became a matter of what you actually saw yourself in many cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But there were, indeed, sitreps, situation reports, from the UN, isn't it, regarding the situation in the whole of Bosnia and also particular parts of it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we never saw those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would like to show you the report also used yesterday, D903?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can place it on Sanction for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I wonder if it's necessarily then to place it also on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. If it's put on Sanction, Mr. Wubben, I see no use -- no need to have it also on the ELMO. I would take it that the members of the public and the persons we have in the strangers' gallery can still follow if it's on Sanction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Exhibit D903.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, Captain, to page 3 under 3(D). Now, this is a report dated the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I still don't see it on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, if it's easier, let's put it on the ELMO and move ahead. Madam Usher, please. And we can still have it on the ELMO in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, we have here a report dated the 22nd of March, 1993, and page 3 out of 7, I quote under -- it's the one, two, three, fourth part of it starting with the word "comment" and the last sentence I quote. "If the Serbs decide to press who the attack -- hoe the attack, the BiH army will not be able to hold out for long. Civilian casualties will be very high." This is regarding the situation in Srebrenica. Isn't it true that the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, sorry to interrupt you, because -- but we can't follow you. You said four on page three?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I said the fourth part of it. If I used the word "paragraph" then you would immediately jump --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why. And there is on the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Should I quote again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I could remember the words, but I couldn't see it in print.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In this quoted sentence you will notice the vital role of the BiH army. Did you became aware of that vital role of the BiH army when you were actually in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- one moment. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, precisely. I'm not surprised the witness cannot follow. There's no reference to the "vital role" of the BiH army in that sentence. So that's certainly not what that sentence states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please restrict your question, Mr. Wubben, to whether the witness knew of the existence of the BiH army at the time or not, because that's what is written -- or that's what that particular sentence contains anyway, reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to the existence as such of a BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In the sentence there's a mentioning of the BiH army. Captain, were you aware of such a BiH army, as mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of a BiH army in Sarajevo because we dealt with what was the beginnings of the BiH army, but that's it from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So in your opinion it is incorrect that the BiH army will not be able to hold out for long if the Serbs decide to press continuing the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't let him answer that question because it doesn't follow from what is written there. If he told you that he is aware or he was aware at the time of the existence of a BiH army in Sarajevo, he cannot -- he cannot confirm or deny whether there was a BiH army in Srebrenica, too. I mean, it's -- how can he answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will make that conclusion at another occasion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In fact, you were not aware of a BiH army in Srebrenica? That's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What was the information you received on arriving at Srebrenica from your team leader regarding the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening of the 27th when those military observers extracted themselves from Konjevic Polje he told me the stories of what had happened that day, where they had been held, essentially, hostage by the women and children and the fact that there was really no Bosnian military to do anything about the situation; and then the Bosnian Serb forces walking the mortars in on the crowd to try and get the military observers out of their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. Yes, you stated that yesterday. Let me focus on Srebrenica and the wider area around this town. What was the assessment of that situation when it comes to warring parties?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assessment that was that the Bosnian Serb forces were pushing and that when they left Konjevic Polje that day, that it was about to fall, based on what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And the front line was near Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the front line was in that area, that day, at Konjevic Polje. That was the Bosnian holding, so that would have been the -- their line of confrontation. By the 27th of March, when we went in, that's when we realised where the new front line was, at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was at the other side of that line of confrontation near Potocari, in your opinion? The other side from the -- the Serbs one side, the other side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in many cases we would see civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Only civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If he could finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My definition of a civilian or a soldier, of course, would be different when I was there. Anybody who carried a weapon I would refer to as a soldier. What we saw civilians in civilian clothing with weapons; if you want to call them a soldier, they're defending their homes, their family, their land. But if you want to define a soldier as somebody in uniform, there was very few people that were in uniforms. And if they were in uniforms, it was something that they may have gotten off a dead soldier or at an army surplus store or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll address that issue later of the uniforms. Let's go further to the military actions by Muslim forces in 1992. Were you aware of the attack by Muslim forces on the village of Ratkovici in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the by Muslim forces on Jezestica in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the attack of Muslim forces on Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the attack by Muslim forces on Bjelovac in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And lastly, the attacks by Muslim forces on Kravica, Siljkovici and Jezestica in January 1992 -- 1993, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You were not aware that Bosnian forces were able to achieve from the summer of 1992 until 1993 that they extended their area of control?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not because operating in a different area and had different missions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So your knowledge about Muslim forces or fighters regarding Srebrenica and the area only stems from March 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Srebrenica area. Yes, in March, April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit D902, Captain. It's a report of the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Sanction is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You can see it on the monitor, Captain?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will quote page 6 paragraph 9(b). "Since approximately May 1992, the BSA has conducted a systematic village-by-village campaign to ethnically cleanse the Cerska-Srebrenica-Zepa enclaves. The predominant threat to the Serbs has been the aggressive attacks by the Muslims against Serb supply lines and villages including pressure against Serbian positions on the Drina River border." You read that, Captain?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: "The reporting period of time from May 1992 includes the attacks mentioned by me." Do you agree that these attacks by Muslim forces had formed the predominant threat to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, Mr. Wubben, if he's not aware of the existence or of the occurrence of the various alleged Muslim attacks, how can he comment as to whether they constituted a threat to the Serbian -- to the Serbs or to the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He might learn from sitreps, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- that the outcome is a pressure -- rather, the basis for such pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you asking him to learn from sitreps? The sitreps say what they say and that's it. I mean, if he isn't even aware of the existence of those attacks, how can he learn anything, as you put it, from the sitreps?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he might give his comment regarding specific information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can't give a comment, Mr. Wubben, if he's not aware of the existence or of the occurrence of those attacks. He can only confirm what -- that he can -- that what the sitrep says, but that's about it. More than that, he cannot go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- in 9(b) what I quoted includes attacks by Muslims against Serb villages, and those villages shouldn't be the same, definitely the same, as the village that I referred to and requested him to and give comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then put to him the question of whether he is aware of any other Muslim attacks against Serbian lines or Serbian villages apart from the ones that he has already told us he was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, can you shed light on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During the period in question, starting from May 1992 until you basically arrived in Srebrenica on the 27th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I spent the first six months - just to recap from yesterday - in Croatia. I had no idea what was going on in Bosnia because that was not my mission. I had a set mission at that time. I did not, and it was not my job, to read sitreps, nor did we get sitreps from the UN forces. It was our job to create sitreps and pass them up. Then I spent the next four and a half months from mid-November 1992 until March 1993 in Sarajevo. That was a completely situation, and I focussed on that situation and only that situation. It was only towards the end of that time when somebody said, You are now posted to Tuzla, that I started thinking about what was going on there. I would be briefed when I got there. And when I ended up staying in the Zvornik bridge and going to Srebrenica, then I dealt with that situation at the time. So I cannot comment on this statement here. Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And the part of the statement in which you yesterday testified about the Drina River border, does that also include that you can give comment on the pressure against Serbian positions on the Drina border of the river?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pressure on the Serbian positions by --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From them or somebody from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: From Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. I could not comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And you have no information regarding?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Other than you gave yesterday of the positions you saw dug-in to prevent any attacks from the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No -- again, it wasn't -- when he mentioned the positions, the dug-in positions yesterday - I will give you an opportunity to speak, Mr. Jones - he specifically mentioned that that was to cut off the approach to the Tuzla area for the Muslims that were trying to move from -- I can't remember exactly which part. But the area he pointed out to us yesterday, he marked on the map, which was literally riddled with these dug-in posts by the Serb was to make sure that no Muslim would manage to pass through and that they would be killed in the process of trying to. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And it is also mentioned in his evidence yesterday that there was heavy artillery on the Serbian side of the Drina. He certainly didn't say, as Mr. Wubben is suggesting, that those were to prevent attacks from the enemy side. Those were heavy guns which were firing towards to Srebrenica, for who knows what reason, to terrorise this population. He didn't say it was in order to prevent attacks; that's Mr. Wubben's interpretation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones, and you are correct on that, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I clarify something here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes of course. You're here to clarify as many things as possible..

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 99.9 per cent of the time all forces that we dealt with tried to hide things from us because they didn't want us to see it. So, I mean, if that puts -- puts it in perspective. We had to dig and patrol and try to find things out, and that's not very easy to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed with your question. In the meantime, Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, when you speak of forces, "99.9 per cent of the time the forces we dealt with were trying to hide things from us," what forces do you mean? Serbian forces or Muslim forces as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim forces, Serbian forces, when I was in Croatia, Croatian forces, Bosnian Serb forces, Serb forces, all the different factions I dealt with in my 12 months there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben, sorry for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, regarding that dug-in position, artillery position, there might be a misunderstanding. What I really meant was another situation. I will come back to that question later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase your question in any way you like, but make sure it reflects the witness's testimony of yesterday and also his clarification of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Referring to those sitreps I already showed you, is it to your knowledge accurate these sitreps?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: These sitreps are a reflection of information that we get. In many cases this information could be second or third hand. And one of the things that the UN really pushes these days is actually having in the sitrep where you say "unconfirmed" or "confirmed." I don't see that in this report, so a lot of this stuff could be based on people hearing stuff. So it's not 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, let me conclude on this myself. Are you in a position, Captain, to confirm to us the correctness or the accuracy of sitrep reports on matters the existence of which you're not aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move to another sitrep report, and I will bear in mind that the witness will only ask for his knowledge regarding the issues he might have seen. And please correct me if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Wubben, I correct you only if there is need to. Otherwise, --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I am not here to teach you your job. You are professional and you know as much as anyone else, if not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I show the witness D904, sitrep 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Captain, this is a report dated the 29th of March, so this refers to a date later an their arrival in the area. There is page 2, paragraph 3, a reference to BiH local commanders attempted to hold the line, referring to Srebrenica. Is that correct to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this would be correct to my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And BiH local commanders, does that refer to the TO and or the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question should be how he understands what he understands those words to mean. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because his conclusion might differ with -- from that of the person who drew up this report in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What do you mean by BiH local commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody who has to take charge if you're being attacked by an opposite force. So a local commander could be the strongest person in the village or the senior guy. And whether they were military or civilian, somebody took over and possibly might be called a commander, but I did not see any structure, as such, when I went into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I quote further down that paragraph: "Fighting was reported in and around Zeleni Jadar with the Serbs in the town itself on the 25th of March. As of the 27th of March, however, the town was still in BiH hands." Can you confirm that to your knowledge, especially the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that when I was wounded on the 3rd of March that Zeleni Jadar was not in Bosnian Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, you stated that you were wounded on the 3rd of -- it's noted as 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 3rd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's for the record. I continue on quoting, Captain, in paragraph 3, the same page. "As the Serb drive continued to collapse the enclaves towards the centre, there was a perceptible hardening of the BiH defence." Can you confirm that to my knowledge when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. I'm not really sure what they're talking about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it true to your knowledge, and I quote further: "Local authorities still appear to be in control and continue to rotate troops to the front line?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. I didn't really see anything as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And have no information received about it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: "The Muslim southern defence line appears at this juncture to hinge on Zeleni Jadar." Can you confirm that to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had received information through my team leader that Zeleni Jadar was a key area, due to it being the last village prior to, I guess, coming into Srebrenica. That was just information that I received. I had gone on foot patrol there, and then eventually went down there on the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When it comes to defence line, I will return to that issue of those Serb artillery placement. And to prevent any misunderstanding, I will quote from the transcript, page 26, of your statement by yesterday. That was on the Serbian side of the Drina, if you might recall, during the time that you were near Zvornik. The question was: "Q. And again, if you can indicate on the map where you saw the artillery placements," you marked it. "Q. So, that's on the Serbian side of the Drina, south of Ljubovija. Is that correct?" Your answer: "Yes, there was a big open area along the river there and they were dug-in in that location, that vicinity." "And what does that indicate," was the question "if artillery is dug-in?" "If artillery are dug-in it is to protect them. You want to get below ground, so that if you are fired on by artillery, that you have some protection because even tanks and guns and, of course, the personnel are vulnerable. So you want to dig-in."

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you said. Now, when it comes to the use by you of the word "enemy artillery" to protect from, what do you mean by that? Who is the enemy out there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA or the VJ were a professional military force, and that would be standard operating procedure to do that. So if the question was: Were they dug-in for hardening, they would do that as a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Anyhow, even without an enemy?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I now turn to Exhibit D900 -- sorry, D894. That's the report of the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is your own report that you were shown yesterday, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, before I proceed on that I'll return to my question. I apologise that I have to return to my latest question. It is, and I quote again the question: "Now when it comes to the use by you of the word "enemy artillery" to protect from, what do you mean by that, who is the enemy out there? Can you please, for the record, give me your answer who's the enemy for the JNA or Serb forces for that side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I use the term "enemy" that's just a term as a military officer that I use. If I'm against somebody, they're my enemy. That's the term that I used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I mean, it's obvious from -- I submit, from yesterday but certainly from what the witness is saying today is that he was speaking generally about artilleries dug-in against enemy attack. Mr. Wubben is trying to elicit from this witness the answer that the enemy of the VJ were the Bosnians so that he can there -- then reach the proposition that the JNA was dug-in against the Muslim attack. And the witness is not saying that and he should not be, well, sort of led into saying something which clearly that's not what his evidence was. His evidence was, in general terms artillery is dug in against enemy attack. It was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has already confirmed that. I don't think we need to bother about this any further, Mr. Wubben, unless you want to pursue it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me state, I thought it was an appropriate question, a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, that's why I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What my learned friend did was giving guidance to the witness and that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. The witness has already stated that the digging in was a matter of normal military practice, irrespective and independent of the existence or the probability or possibility of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I object to any suggestion that I'm trying to give guidance to the witness. That's completely inappropriate. If as a matter of common sense I restate what this witness has stated repeatedly, but which is being ignored by Mr. Wubben, then that's certainly not guidance, it's simply setting the matter straight for everybody's benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this witness is one of those witnesses that doesn't need guidance from either of you, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Captain, if I may proceed, it's correct you can see in front of you on the monitor, I hope, yes, your report referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On the first page, and I quote, and it's down one, two, three, four, five lines, I quote: "The Serbs were attacking on all sides and slowly squeezing the pocket smaller and smaller, looting and then burning the Muslim homes as they went." Did you actually saw your yourself this burning and looting by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on the 3rd of April I actually was an eyewitness to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that looting and burning had been committed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Serb forces that I saw doing that in that particular village that I discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And by making use of your binoculars you were able to identify the looting?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also the burning?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually see anybody with a match, but the village was on fire that we observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And how did you conclude that those forces were burning down those houses?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You make a conclusion there; there's something -- the homes are on fire, so you make a deduction that they must have done it. That's not a hundred per cent, but that's a deduction that you make.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you learn any burning down of houses by the Bosnian army at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of that, but of course it was quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which period of time, Mr. Wubben? I think you need to put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When did you learn that information regarding burning down of houses by the Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. It's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was the third Bosnian side, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I thought he already stated the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During the duration of your stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even to put it back a little bit further, I seen thousands of homes in a state of destruction and that had been burned in former Yugoslavia over my 12 months. Who did that or how they did that, in many cases I can only speculate. In many cases I actually saw it happening in Sarajevo. In the area of Srebrenica in that period, I only saw it on that day, the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And yesterday you were also referring to children in Srebrenica without parents, wandering around, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you witness any such children torching houses or attempting to burn houses down?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you witness any houses burning down in Srebrenica during your stay?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Also, despite the cluster bomb casings that you actually saw when you were in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask that again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica, you testified that someone brought in to you the cluster come casing. And given that cluster bomb casing, you -- and the remainders of it, you actually did not saw any damage or burning from it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just saw the cluster bomb casings. In fact they were in the PTT when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will go now to your report, second part, Captain, and that's on the second page, and I quote: "Shelling" -- no. It's the fifth line. "Near the village Zeleni Jadar, Bosnian soldiers were massing for an attack." What do you mean by "Bosnian soldiers were massing for attack"? Can you give more information about that, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning I had been on a radio communications to get a convoy in at -- closer to Srebrenica. And we had discussed going to Zeleni Jadar after the radio check that morning to try to check on the situation. And there was fresh shelling going on. There had been a more or less cease-fire prior to the 3rd of April. And when I got down to Zeleni Jadar there was 1 or 200 men in civilian uniforms. Yes, in this document I say "soldiers" because they were carrying weapons. At that time to me anybody with a weapon was a soldier, as I mentioned earlier. They appeared to be massing for attack because Zeleni Jadar was under artillery fire. In actual fact, I would say, they were actually getting ready to withdraw because they don't have any trenches or any place to hide and artillery is going to kill them, so they would most likely withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And those Bosnian soldiers, you notice how they implemented an attack or fulfilled a combat action?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they withdrew. I went up on top of the hill, I was hit by the mortar, and I was Med-Evac'ed out of there. By the end of that day I was told the Bosnian Serb forces were within spitting distance of Srebrenica, which means they were within one or two kilometres of the centre of the town. So they had advanced approximately eight to ten that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You were brought to the hospital of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was that a war hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by a war hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In military terms.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were the soldiers, the fighters, brought into that hospital whenever wounded?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on who was brought there. There was civilians brought there, anybody who was wounded was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Including fighters and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any fighters or soldiers go in there. I went in there two times, once on a patrol. There was -- we didn't actually see anybody in the rooms, we didn't go in the rooms. And when I was wounded, I was operated on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did the hospital fulfil a central role for the area as a surgeon for wounded?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only medical treatment that anybody could receive, in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I will end with a quotation, Captain, at the end of your report. It's -- and I quote from the third line on the second page below: "Maybe when each faction has cleansed the area of concern and gets the land and recognition they want, then there might be a relative peace." Captain, what do you mean by this concluding or last sentence?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the different factions had some types of maybe historical land lines where they felt that they owned. I know the Bosnian Serbs were trying to tie-in numbers of land areas with the Krajina and Croatia in Bosnia, and then tie it into one continuous area which would be part of what has been termed "Greater Serbia." The Croatians had some historical-tie land areas in Bosnia. They were trying to tie that in so that it could be tied as one areas into Croatia. And, of course, the Bosnians had areas. So everybody was trying to just tidy up the areas that they wanted so that there wouldn't be separate areas, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "cleanse," cleanse the area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cleanse the area could be just simply pushing people out so that they're no longer there, so that physically flee. It could be to kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So both parties, both sides, Bosnian forces or Serb forces, whenever they do an action like that, that's your understanding of cleansing?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, cleansing could -- like I said, in many cases cleansing was just trying to maybe even intimidate people to leave verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly it was the reference to both sides. The witness has been talking about Croatia, Croatian Serbs -- sorry, Croatians, Serbians, and Bosnians. He's obviously talking about the whole situation in the former Yugoslavia. He's not talking about this particular area, the Srebrenica enclave. So I would object to referring to both sides when we're actually talking about three sides. And also just I don't see the relevance of this line of questioning. I don't know on what the overall political objectives, how they have any relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, its relevance, I'm satisfied, we are satisfied. As to the other point that you mentioned, the report is dealing with a specific situation. And the final part of the report to which he has been referred is after all his own. I don't think it has anything to do with Croatia and that. It's an assessment that he is making at this point and he's being asked to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, no, indeed, Your Honour, and the sentence before would have made that clear. "One year in a combat zone is definitely enough for the time being." That's referring to his whole mission in the former Yugoslavia, which is -- included staying in Karlovac in Croatia and, in the answer he's just given, he was referring to the general situation in the whole of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in any case the question deals with the question of cleansing, what is meant by cleansing. And I think we haven't moved an inch, basically, from where we started when the question was put in the first place because he's given an answer and that's it. Do you want to pursue the matter any further, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have concluded that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. I will move to Srebrenica itself, the town of Srebrenica, and its buildings. Yesterday you gave testimony regarding -- also today regarding the PTT building. What kind of building was that? Can you describe it.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT building is the -- I guess PTT stands for post, telegraph, and telephone. It was a square building, three -- I believe three storeys, as I recall, three levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was its function?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its function?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At the time that you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took over and it was supposed to be our UN headquarters. Like I said we put a UN flag up on the roof and we were using it to be our UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You stated "we took over." Were you the only users of that building?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As far as you know. Might it be true that also Muslim forces or civilians may use -- made use of that PTT building at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point during my time in Srebrenica, actually close to the 3rd of April, I heard there was a ham radio somewheres in the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who made use of that ham radio?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you make use of it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Or someone of the team refer to you as making use of that ham radio?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So you were not aware that the PTT building also functioned as a communication facility for the Muslim forces at a time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. On the 3rd of April when I was wounded I heard that there was a ham radio somewheres on the third floor, and the information was put out to the world press that I had been wounded. And that's -- that was the first I heard of it, and I left the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And across the street of that PTT building there is the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you notice there beside of that hospital a tank?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw a tank near the hospital, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you observe any shooting, outside shooting, from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside shooting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: By heavy weaponry, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you heard of the Domavija Hotel? Did you see it, that hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. I may have seen the building, but that name does not come into my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the headquarters of Hakija Meholjic, a leader within the Bosnian Serb -- sorry, the Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Whenever the PTT building is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up, Mr. Wubben, because we have two questions in one. Did you ever hear of Hakija Meholjic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not heard that name, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then the second part of the questions then automatically falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I continue with this question. Did you have any other local commander, local commander, in the time you have been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only person that we dealt with is that liaison officer, which -- his picture was shown us yesterday, and I heard the name Naser Oric when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request to make -- I have to re-organise, and it will definitely not be a disadvantage for the scheduling of today. So I prefer, if possible, if possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To have the break now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- to have the break now rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Mr. Wubben. So we will have a 40-minute break starting from now. It will give an opportunity to Judge Brydensholt to meet with his -- some of his co-national researchers. Then we will continue afterwards and you will have all the time to finish. All right? Thank you. So let's say we'll meet at exactly quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, I have a question for you regarding your stay in Srebrenica as an UNMO at the time in the team you're in and colleagues involved. Do you recall at the time a person called Jamie?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Captain Trevor Jamie, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What was his task at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the operations officer for the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Had he any responsibilities for the UNMOs as an operations officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the jobs of an operations officer is to assess tasks and possibly give tasks to people, based on what the team leader might give him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So it would be important for Captain Jamie to be fully briefed on situations in Srebrenica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be his job. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did Jamie have also there access to sitreps?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to answer that question. As an operations officer, that would be entirely possible; however, I do not believe we had access to any sitreps when we were in there because we had very poor communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yesterday you testified about Muslim forces. I will quote from page 53, and I notice that you speak about -- testify about Bosnian forces. When we use the terminology "Bosnian forces" or "Muslim forces," can we agree that these are the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in the sitreps the BiH army, BiH forces, is alike, the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one of the terms used as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. "Well, the Bosnian Serb forces didn't have a lot of infantry, but they had a lot of or a lot more of artillery and tanks and equipments, whereas the Bosnian forces had tens thousands of men that could fight; however, they didn't have a lot of artillery and tanks, even small arms they didn't have a lot of." Is that correct? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, they didn't have a lot of artillery and tanks, so they did have tanks? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question is where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. The question is not where. The question is: If they didn't have a lot of artillery and tanks, my next question is: So they did have tanks, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen tanks on the Bosnian side, but they had been captured by -- or from the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb forces. So on a very limited basis they may have had a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So anyhow, they had some tanks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Wubben. Yes, he's answered that question. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's completely unclear whether we're talking about the whole of Bosnia or we're talking about Srebrenica. I don't know if Mr. Wubben wants to keep it vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that needs to be clarified, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Then how do you know? Where have you seen those?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In Srebrenica also?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica I saw one tank that had been -- I wouldn't say it was captured. I think it was destroyed and abandoned by the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And around Srebrenica, a wider area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you also notice artillery?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Owned by which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: By the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no artillery that I saw on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's specify. We're talking of the Srebrenica area and its overall ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was no artillery on the Bosnian side in the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As you noticed during your stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will get back to that issue later on, sir. I will quote further. Please bear me a moment. I will, in general, refer to your testimony yesterday when you testified that there were not many uniforms within Muslim forces or fighters wearing civilian clothes rather than uniform. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- any Bosnian fighter that I ever saw was wearing mostly civilian clothing. There may have been bits and pieces of a uniform that they had got from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you gave testimony about the function of the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For the morale, unity. And isn't it true that uniforms make also a distinction whenever there is a combat operation not to fire against each other?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, this function of distinction is very important during combat action, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extremely important, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can it be true that distinctions can also be made by other forms than by way of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For example, by ribbons?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ribbons. Of course, that could be a way to distinguish, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Bandages around the head?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Bandages around arm?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And couldn't that be enough for an armed group to operate in a combat action?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be enough, but there's -- I would not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So you can be a fighting force without having uniforms, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let him answer the question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and I do not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, well, the witness is being asked about the particular purpose of uniforms in order to make sure that fighters don't shoot each other. And now it's being taken as if for all purposes one can have an armed group without uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection overruled. It's a very pertinent question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Though it's limited to that one specific function, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is at this point, but it's a very pertinent question and, of course, I will allow it. Please proceed, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On that issue that was enough. I will move to another issue, that's the acquiring of food within the town. That was a very poor situation, isn't it, for the civilians, for everyone, fighters alike.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you notice how the Bosnian armed forces acquired food in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it at your time in Srebrenica right to say that to a certain extent the Serbian armed forces also should take their share from food droppings?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody that was in Srebrenica that didn't have food was entitled to their share of food, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show on Sanction Exhibit D700, a video, famine situation, an ABC Washington documentary including introduction and report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, the video starts rolling at 1 minute, 13 seconds point 6 -- 13 seconds. And could we raise the sound a little bit because I can barely -- I can hear what she is saying but I could hear better if the sound is raised a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I prefer to start at 1.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... in Bosnia has witnessed the impact of the airdrops. "These scenes come to us from the town of Srebrenica, a place almost impossible to get to. ABC's Tony Birtley finally managed it last week, in what can be described as a heroic effort to describe what's happening in Srebrenica. Tony travelled by" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Reporter: American planes have -- in Bosnia has witnessed the impact of the air drops. "These scenes come to us from the town of Srebrenica, a place almost impossible to get to. ABC's Tony Birtley finally managed it last week in what can only be described as an heroic effort to let us see what's happening in Srebrenica. Tony travelled by ..." "Tony Birtley: American planes have successfully dropped aid into this area for the last five nights running. The villagers say they received only one prepared lunch packet, the rest have been --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meanwhile because there should be a little bit longer, the report by the person who is ten seconds and -- it was around eight seconds. So we need some moments to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Tony Birtley: Planes have successfully air dropped aid into this area for the last five nights running. The villagers say the received only one prepared lunch packet. The rest has been taken by the army. "Most people have been eating only bread" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sir, you were able to listen and see the report made by this journalist?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with this journalist. I understand what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And you understood what he said?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What did he mean by "one prepared lunch packet and the rest taken by the army"?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant. I just know what he said. I was not there during that particular videotaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you ever there during the air dropping of food?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you see a familiar situation? Civilians taking food and the rest taken by the army?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The rations were dropped out of C-130 Hercules. They landed up on the hilltop outside of Srebrenica, and then people would go up and try and get the rations. I did not see any distinguish -- there was no distinguishing between the military or army or civilians. Just people went up and got the food. They would fight for the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Whoever arrived?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever got up there first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Whoever arrived or so has an advantage, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is the end of this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the record, the screening ends at 3 minutes 07 seconds point 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica, sir, did you -- you did never go to the SUP building, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The SUP building.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the headquarters of the army?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to any headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you -- you did never go to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware there was military police, so I would not be able to go to a building as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would move now to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's the final issue. It's about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you aware of this demilitarisation agreement dated the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the agreement. I have never actually seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Part of the agreement is the disarming of the Muslim forces, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show now the witness a new exhibit. It's a report of the 21st of April, 1993. It bears an ERN number 00452158 up to 004125 -- sorry, I will repeat. 00452168, ten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Captain, this is a report on demilitarisation of Srebrenica dated the 21st of April, 1993, first page. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On the subsequent page and then one of the -- there is the mentioning of -- in paragraph under (a), the second line "weapons have been placed in custody of UNPROFOR." Are you aware that this is -- has been the implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware according to this -- reading this document. I was wounded on the 3rd of April. I spent 30 days recovering, so I was not in theatre during that time, so I have no idea what happened other than reading this now and having been told that this agreement was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll move now to a page bears ERN 00452162. And under paragraph three in the middle, and I quote: "With the present UNPROFOR force level, UNPROFOR cannot control the movement of weapons in the confrontation area of Srebrenica and beyond. So we must regard the solution found today as a symbolic first step." Now, sir, do you read -- can you read that part that I quoted?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica some weeks prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think really for the record and for the public and for the witness to ignore the fact that this is a remark of the Bosnian Serb representative and just to quote it out of context is improper. And this is a remark by the Bosnian Serb representative, and that should be clear for everyone, otherwise there might be a confusion on the part of, as I say, the witness and the public and the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I abide by the rule not -- I abide by the rule by this Trial Chamber not to state who quotes something -- who states something but ask for a comment regarding a certain quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I don't think that rule applies to what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a document which is supposed -- on the face of it, on the face of it, looks as if it is a report, official report, of the headquarters. And it does contain the positions taken by the two sides. So if what you quoted is in the report only in that it is a report of the position taken by one of the sides, it must be put to -- if not to the witness, who can read it himself, it must be made clear to the members of the public that you're not reading, as such, from the assessment of whoever drafted this report, but from the assessment of one of the parties involved. So that, I think, Mr. Jones is perfectly right. The witness, I think, is aware of it. But members of the public are certainly not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I intended to finally make a kind of concluding remark on it rather than a question. But I will now include it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sir, in the report, and we see on the same page, the Bosnian Serb representative and then a remark referred and linked to the Bosnian Serb representative giving that information. And I quote under 3: "With the present UNPROFOR force level, UNPROFOR cannot control the movement of weapons in the confrontation level of Srebrenica and beyond. So we must regard the solution found today as a symbolic first step." Now, sir, you with your experience in Srebrenica at the time some weeks prior to those remarks, do you have any comment on that? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I agree with which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: With the part that such an agreement can only -- such an agreement must be regarded as a symbolic first step.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. All I can say is that when I was there there was one section of six or seven Canadian soldiers, and later on there was, I believe, a company of soldiers. And they could not -- certainly could not control all the ground. 120 men cannot control that size area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move now to the page bearing ERN number 00452168. Here we have -- do you come to that --

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, this page and a subsequent page, refer to -- according to the header material -- and I quote: "Material delivered to UNPROFOR during demilitarisation of Srebrenica." And there are three columns of dates: 19th of April, 20th of April, 21st of April, and there's a column of total. Now, my question to you is: As it appeared from this report, the material and -- listed is the material delivered to UNPROFOR during those days, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me go through some ten of these listed weaponry and ask you a question whether or not you see any of those weapons, and then I will focus on heavy weaponry. An M-68 APC, did you know of any used by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A light anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I believe I saw it on a news report one time, but I did not physically see that on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, sir, an M-48 mountain gun?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: An anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: 90-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 90-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: M-70 rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 20-millimetre anti-aircraft mount?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 20-millimetre guns?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: An RPG 7 -- but first is it correct that -- yes, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is an RPG so that we can follow better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An RPG is a rocket launcher that can be fired by a soldier and they can reload the rockets as you see them from the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you see any of those?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica I did not see any RPGs, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And around the area of Srebrenica, as used by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The subsequent page. That's ERN 00452169 almost in the middle. 120-millimetre bomb?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is that bomb usually ammunition for a mortar gun?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "bomb" there. 120-millimetre would be consistent with a 120-millimetre mortar. I cannot say from that definition there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And last, an anti-aircraft gun carriage, did you ever saw it in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I noticed you standing --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll deal with it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm tendering, and I request a P number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yaiza, you need to give me the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 594. So this document which is in English, part of which is handwritten and part of which also consists of maps, totalling 12 pages in all, with ERN 00452158 to and including 00452169 is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P594.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please bear me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise, to re-organise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that you didn't know any further local commanders in Srebrenica, didn't you, beside the persons already mentioned by you?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
