utterances.text: And are you familiar with the name Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Zulfo or Tursun?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Or Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's my final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. And, Mr. Jones, I take it that you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, Captain MacDonald, you were shown exhibit D902, and you don't need it in front of you but you recall you were asked about pressure by the Muslims on Serbian supply lines and "Serbian positions on the Drina River border."

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best if you have the document in front of you. It's D902. Turn to page 6, and it's 9(b), and it's the second sentence which you were directed to. "The predominant threat to the Serbs has been the attacks by the Muslims against Serb supply lines and villages including pressure against Serbian positions on the Drina river border."

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I firstly want to ask you this. Firstly, the reference to Serbian positions, does that or not imply military position or something of the military nature, when you see the term "positions."

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, yes, that's what it says there. Serbian positions, that's what I would deduce as a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And supply lines, Serb supply lines, that's obviously a military target, a legitimate military target, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a supply line would be a term for resupply. And if you targeted that, you could acquire supplies, I guess, or destroy supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not that might be a reference to the Serbian supply lines which were keeping up the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to comment on that. I could -- I would only be able to assume that, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how, in your opinion, Srebrenica was under siege at the relevant time and you've also told us how the Serbs were obstructing food in the form of aid convoys going into Srebrenica. I simply want to ask you this: If you're under siege, do you have any option, apart from putting pressure on the besieging forces, or to simply give up and die?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the witness to answer that question, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I would like it if the witness could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you're starving and you have no food and your food supplies have run out, then you're going to have to get food somewheres else and probably use any means to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, moving to a different area, you've told us about what you saw in Zeleni Jadar and how there were homes burning and how you make the deduction, as you put it, that those had been set on fire. I simply want to ask you this: Is that deduction confined, or is it not, to simply what you saw on that day? In other words, that was a deduction you made on that day based on what you saw, but it's not a deduction for all purposes which you would draw when you see burning homes?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I saw that that day, but I had seen the effects of homes that had been either burning or had been burned throughout former Yugoslavia for almost 12 months. So you make deductions based on what you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you were in Sarajevo and you saw burning houses or burning buildings, you didn't draw the same deduction, did you, that it had been human agency; you deducted that it had been caused by artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to deduct it from that point because I saw it happening. If I see a home that had been burned and it's stopped now, then I make a deduction; but when I actually see something happening, then that's an eyewitness account.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you'll draw different deductions depending on what you see, depending on what's firing, depending on a whole host of factors?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And if I would clarify one thing. I did patrol a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of times when Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, and I had seen homes that had been burned or that had been on fire between that fire. How it happened, I don't know. But there was the effects, and we saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm turning to your report now. I'm just letting the interpretation catch up. And it's D894. And you're asked about this reference to cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it in front of him? Has he -- does he have it at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to be sure he does. It's D894. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You'll see it's at the end of the second page. You'll recall there was some discussion or some confusion as to whether your conclusions at the very end, whether that referred to the whole period that you were in former Yugoslavia, the whole period of your mission of one year, or whether you were referring to something specific in the Srebrenica pocket. So if you can clarify for us what your conclusions there are referring to.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was based on things that I had seen in my whole 12 months or at this point, close to the 12 months I had been there, not specifically to the -- just in the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as concerns the Srebrenica area, did you or did you not ever see cleansing, ethnic cleansing, by Bosnian Muslims in the Srebrenica pocket?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you or did you not see the Serbian Orthodox church in Srebrenica when you were there, standing, undamaged?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the church and it was not destroyed. It was not damaged. It may have had some small damage to it, but it was still standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hate to interrupt, but I see that there was accidentally two questions within one. We have the word "cleansing" and we have the word "ethnic cleansing." It might mean the same but might also have a different connotation, and --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would prefer two questions rather than one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he, if Mr. Jones intended two things, then, yes, but if he intended one thing, basically "cleansing" meaning "ethnic cleansing," then it stays as -- we'll just have a confirmation from the witness. You know whether you intended two things or one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica, did you ever see Bosnian Muslims there forcing Serbs out of the area using violence?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in general terms, were you aware, firstly, that Serbs were still living in Srebrenica, in the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have any information on that. It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you aware from your time in Bosnia that there were high-ranking members, officers of the Bosnian army who were Serbs and Croats, and not necessarily of Muslim nationality?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, at one point you were asked about whether Muslim forces and -- sorry, whether Bosnian, the term "Bosnian" referred to Bosnian Muslims, whether that in turn might be interchangeable with the Bosnian army. I want to be very clear about that. Are you saying that -- let me put it this way. You told us that you didn't see the Bosnian army, in the sense of an organised army, in Srebrenica, but you saw Muslim fighters, if you like.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're not saying, are you, that the term "Muslim fighters" is interchangeable with "Bosnian army"?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't -- I really can't say that. You could deduce that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I'm getting at there is this: You've told us, as I said, that you didn't see the Bosnian army in the sense of an organised army in Srebrenica, Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So those are not the same thing, Muslim fighters are not identical with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. What I saw was civilian men that had weapons who were defending themselves, but not necessarily an organised military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked about the use of ribbons in order to -- in order that people in an action might avoid killing people who were on the same side, broadly speaking. And it was suggested to you that that might substitute for a uniform. Now, you told us yesterday that uniforms are important for morale, for recognising different ranks, for discipline, for a command structure. Would you say that ribbons can substitute for all those things? So you didn't need uniforms, ribbons were enough for an organised, disciplined army, or were you say something different?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are historical examples of where people have used other ways to distinguish themselves in lieu of having a uniform. So, yes, ribbons could be used. It would be -- if you have nothing else, if you don't have a uniform, that might be something that you could use to distinguish possibly even a commander or who the soldiers were or different units. It's possible, yes. You could paint faces, which had been done in Scotland, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But firstly, would that be simply for the purpose of that action and for as long as that action endured?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be something that you could put on or take off during that action, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in terms of having different ranks, wouldn't that imply different-coloured ribbons in order to be able to distinguish between, as you said, a commander and someone else? It wouldn't do to have just one colour?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess it would depend on what was available to use. If you had something different and -- the key thing would be that everybody that was working under that commander knew what that distinguishing mark was, same as a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you had a system of using ribbons or bandages, then of course anyone not wearing a ribbon or bandage would not be part of that system. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, of course, if civilians were also wearing ribbons, bandages, et cetera, then the purpose of distinguishing actual fighters from civilians would be lost, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally on this, can you -- can you answer this. If you only had ribbons, no uniforms whatsoever, only ribbons, and no barracks, no charts of organisation, equipment, no system of giving armies, no armoury, no salaries, would you say that -- that nonetheless ribbons are perfectly sufficient to have an organised military structure?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked about a tank which you saw. Are you aware whether the Bosnians actually had shells for those -- for the tank that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have had one or two, but that's certainly not enough. They didn't have fuel, and I believe one of the tracks on that vehicle had been destroyed or damaged as well. So the fact that they had it was of no real use to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly how much a tank round weighs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tank round could weigh up to -- well, 50 kilos -- no, 100 pounds, so, yeah, 50 kilos. It's quite heavy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be right that general resupply of artillery and tank rounds would have to be done by a vehicle, given the heaviness of those missiles?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the biggest difficulties in military operations is resupplies, particularly of artillery and tank rounds because of their weight and their size.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you aware whether the Bosnians in Srebrenica had resupply by road, by lorries, for artillery and tank rounds?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, they had no vehicles. And any resupply that they may have had was done by foot or by mule or donkey, and then on a very limited basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would it be possible to carry hundreds of artillery and tank rounds by mule or donkey from -- I suppose Tuzla would be the nearest spot?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they would probably focus on small-arms ammunition for AK-47s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally on this document you were shown concerning demilitarisation, I appreciate that you were not there and therefore there's a limited amount you can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But nonetheless if the witness could be shown P594, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you firstly to turn to the last two pages -- in fact, before you go there, I want to direct your attention to the following page. So one moment, please. Yes, it's page -- it's the second page and it's 3(f). And it refers to the fact of the town of Srebrenica should agree to be a demilitarised area. Now, is it correct from that, and perhaps is it your own understanding, that the agreement concerned an area which was to be demilitarised, as opposed to a side, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression that the area out to eight kilometres from the centre part of Srebrenica was the area to be demilitarised, as they term it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when we turn to this list at the end, material delivered to UNPROFOR during demilitarisation of Srebrenica, you -- firstly, it doesn't say that these were delivered by the Bosnian Muslims or by the Bosnian Serbs, does it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we don't know from this document who delivered this material to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it doesn't say either, does it, whether any of these weapons were actually functioning, simply that they were delivered?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what you told us about problems of resupply for artillery rounds and tank shells, would that apply to the ammunition required for any of the heavy artillery which we see listed there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you were asking there. Can you rephrase that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In this list your attention was drawn to various items of heavy artillery. As far as the Bosnian Muslims are concerned, would your comments about the difficulty of resupply apply for those weapons, too?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any of the weapons that are in this list, there would be great difficulties in re supplying, even if they had the ammunition for those particular types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe when you were in Croatia you worked, actually, on demilitarisation issues. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of my main tasks during that time, during those six months that I was in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I want to direct your attention to page 2, and it's 3(b). It's the first sentence. "There was insufficient time to do more than tour the area by vehicle in order to satisfy both sides that the area contained no military formations or personnel." Now, firstly, would you understand from that that a tour was conducted in order to satisfy both sides that there was indeed no military formations or personnel?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the jobs of the military observers or the protection force troops would be to familiarise themselves with the area. It says here they didn't have time, so they would have tried to do as much as they could based on the amount of time, to see what they could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this agreement has been signed, in fact, hasn't it? A demilitarisation agreement was signed by both representatives?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by the commanding officer of the Canadian Battalion, the Bosnian Serb rep, and the Bosnian Muslim rep.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from your experience of demilitarisations, would that be a common feature, that there should be no military formations or personnel within the demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally on this theme you told us -- you said that 120 men, i.e., the Canadian Infantry Company who came in, couldn't control the area. May we take it from that that -- nor could they defend the area against any attack from the verbs? They wouldn't be in a position to do so successfully?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR forces were sent in to former Yugoslavia with self-defence pretty much only. So if they were attacked, they certainly would defend themselves. But if there was an overwhelming force, then 120 men would have a difficult time with the limited amount of weapons that they had to defend themselves. Because the forces were supposed to have cease-fire, so they're not supposed to attack you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And 1995 proved, in fact, that it wasn't possible for the UN to protect this area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Judge Brydensholt, do you have any questions? Yes. Judge Brydensholt would like to put a question to you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: We saw a picture of your liaison officer or person to the authorities in Srebrenica. How was he introduced to you? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He -- he came to the PTT and said that he would be our liaison officer. I remember talking to him. He was not from Srebrenica. He had come from -- in fact, he had been living outside of former Yugoslavia in some other country and had actually come back to, as he had put it, to fight or to help out with his people's cause. So who he was working for or how he came to be in Srebrenica exactly, I'm not sure. But he came and said he would be our go-between. And that's essentially how I dealt with people on -- for most of the year that I worked in former Yugoslavia, through a liaison officer, whether it was Croat forces in Croatia, the Serbian Krajina, Sarajevo, and Serb forces, Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did he stay in the PTT building as well? Did he live there, I mean, or did he live other places?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know where he lived. He did not stay in the PTT building as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And I take it that you don't know to who he reported?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not the team leader for the military observers. I had other tasks. So the team leader may have known a lot more. I assume he would have known a lot more. I just talked to this guy a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Captain MacDonald, I just have a follow-up question. Have you been aware of any negotiations going on, either in the PTT building or in any other building?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Negotiations between UNPROFOR and people from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary task during the, I guess, week or eight days I was in there was to negotiate convoys of humanitarian aid in from the Bosnian Serb side to the confrontation line, into Srebrenica. That was the main task at that time. So -- I spent most of my time conducting either foot patrols, vehicle patrols, or radio communications. That was my main task. So that's why I didn't have a lot of dealings with any personnel. I spent a lot of time up on the hill above Srebrenica trying to talk to military observers outside of the pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But if there have been negotiations going on, there must have been two sides, and have you any idea who had been on the Muslim side within these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was not aware, not involved in that. Also, another key thing to think about. We did not have computers or anything at that time. If you think back to 1992, 1993, we had very limited computers. So if the team leader had a lot of stuff up in his mind and he didn't brief us, then, you know, he had it. We only had one meeting. There was so much chaos in Srebrenica at that time for us, we had one meeting on the 2nd of April, and then of course I was wounded the next day and Med-Evac'ed on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, just for the sake of clarification I would like to ask you. You spoke of defence lines. I think one was in the wider area of Konjevic Polje, another one was closer to Potocari. How would you describe, according to your experience or the actual knowledge, how would a defence line consist of? How would it be built up?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: A defence line may not be built-up at all. It may just be -- it could be anything. If you think about a line of confrontation, there is no set distance between two forces. It's all based on mostly terrain. Sometimes two can -- opposing forces could be within metres of each other. Other times, based on terrain, it could be kilometres. When I was in Srebrenica, we were not aware of any actual defensive positions dug. I don't -- I wouldn't say they had the equipment to do that. And because of the fluid action where there may have been movement back and forth, it's not possible to continuously dig in. So a line of confrontation may simply be where somebody is. And you can move very quickly. You can fall back to a new location, or if you can attack, it will change. So we were just aware of the line at that point, being Konjevic Polje on the 12th of April; then when we went in and we actually came up to the spot where we saw Bosnian Serb forces, then it was -- now a deduction, this is now the line. And in between you might be able to see the distance, where the next checkpoint is for whatever forces or whoever might be guarding on the other side. It could be a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So would you agree that instead of defence line we should -- you could also or perhaps even better speak of confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We normally use line of confrontation as the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, coming back to your own report, that is D894, and I don't think we need you to put it on the ELMO. You wrote "near the village Zeleni Jadar, the Bosnian soldiers were massing for an attack." That's your wording. Now, we already clarified that when you spoke of soldiers you meant it in terms of any people, including civilians wearing weapons, regardless whether being uniformed or not.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, what do you mean with "massing"?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there was 1 or 200 men all bunched up together. And when I say "massing," they're gathering to do something. Whether it's an attack or maybe withdraw, I don't know. The -- all I do know is when I got up on top of the hill, Zeleni Jadar was under shell fire from 122-millimetre artillery. And if you're not dug in, as I just mentioned, and all you've got is rifles, then at that point you can deduce that they're either getting ready to do an attack, a counter-attack. If somebody comes into the forces -- if the Bosnian Serb forces are going to attack into Zeleni Jadar, they have to lift their artillery, otherwise they're going to get injured. So this force that we saw was either going to then do one of two things. They were either going to wait for the artillery to lift and then counter-attack as the Bosnian Serb forces came into Zeleni Jadar, or they were going to withdraw to safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of gathering. Is this gathering to be understood as purely accidental or that it was some sort of coordination or to come -- to get together and to form either defensive attack or some other action?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Zeleni Jadar was deemed to be a key intersection. How coordinated it was, I cannot give you any information on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. That brings your testimony to an end, Captain MacDonald. For the record, your surname is Mac, M-a-c, and then Donald, the two parts together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So that's for -- I knew it was like that, but for the record I want to make sure that it is entered correctly. Yes, I thank you, Captain. Your testimony ends here. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on my own behalf and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case as a Defence witness. Our usher, together with the rest of the staff of this Tribunal now, will assist you and finalise arrangements for your return to wherever your destination is. And on behalf of everyone present here, I should like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's -- I need to talk to you for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number one, it seems that this witness has finished one day ahead of schedule. Thursday, as I explained yesterday, we would have had the problem of the plenary and we could have shifted the sitting to the afternoon, but we needed two hours. In any case, it seems that we are not sitting. Is there a possibility of your bringing over a witness who could start either on Thursday or Friday, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's too bad. All right. May I remind you of a couple of things. I think end of this week, Friday we are to expect from you any indication of any witnesses you would like to bring back; that's number one. There was another deadline involved. You also need to respond to the Prosecution filing as soon as you can so that we can deal with this matter at the earliest. If you can file it by tomorrow, then it is quite possible that I will -- of course, it's my two colleagues agree. If there is need to discuss the matter, that we try and convene on Friday. However, I need to discuss this with my two colleagues first. So if there are problems relating to disclosure as they might arise from the filing that we've had plus your response, please try to update us by the end of work tomorrow. And then we will try and contact you later on. The other thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is that you will recall that during the week we were not sitting, we were working, you were working, I, after consultation with my two colleagues, extended the period within which the -- your expert was to finalise his examination of -- by eight days. And I take it that the eight days will lapse or expire tomorrow. I want to make sure that you are in contact with your expert to ensure that this matter is not prolonged any further than what we established so that in addition arrangements can be made by the registry for the recovery of the documents and return -- their return to their -- to the Tribunal, to the Prosecution in particular. The other thing that I wish to tell you is this, that after Friday, after we've had this list from you, if there are witnesses to be brought back, we need to sit down together and make a re-assessment of the situation as it obtains now and, if necessary, review the date by which you are expected to finish your case. So we'll -- my advice is that you start working on this. Try to be as practical and as cooperative as possible. Our responsibility is to try and finish the earliest possible. And for that to happen is to try and avoid repetitive evidence. I think we have come to a stage where both sides should know exactly where, more or less, you stand, where is the strength or the weakness of the Prosecution case and concentrate accordingly. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that spirit last week we -- we conducted a planned revision of our witness list and we were planning to submitted a motion this week to drop some witnesses and add one or two, but with a net saving in any event of quite a few days. So that's something that we should be able to file this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's it. I think I'll come back to you on this -- on all of these matters on Monday when we reconvene. Yes, we are not sitting Monday. Tuesday, or earlier if we need to meet again later on this week on outstanding matters. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.00 p.m.,
